title: One Simple Habit That Will Improve Your Reading
author: Colton Cauthen
summary: Colton Cauthen argues that the most effective and accessible improvement a reader can make is simply jotting down brief notes after each chapter in a book. The practice requires no elaborate system: flip back through the chapter and write down a few things that seem important—new characters or events for fiction, key terms or arguments for nonfiction. Cauthen defends this deliberately simple approach against the instinct to over-engineer it, noting that adding too much friction transforms a useful habit into an abandoned project. The cognitive case for the practice is that these review notes move content from working memory (temporary) to long-term memory (durable) and provide a quick comprehension check. Having a pencil in hand while reading and making simple marks—underlines, asterisks, margin notes—creates visual flags that make the end-of-chapter review fast and effortless. The piece positions this as a foundation for more sophisticated reading practices rather than an endpoint: readers who build this simple habit first are far more likely to develop additional skills over time.
points: After each chapter, briefly jot down what seemed important—new characters, key arguments, a favorite quote—to move content from working memory to long-term memory
Keeping a pen in hand while reading and making simple marks (underlines, asterisks) creates visual flags that make the end-of-chapter review fast and nearly effortless

The deliberate simplicity of the practice is its strength: adding too much friction turns a useful habit into an abandoned system, and five to ten minutes per chapter produces compounding returns over time
quotes: In fact, I think honing the art and craft of reading well is an essential part of the reading life.
However, from my own experience, attempting to force too much progress at once can easily spoil reading by adding in too much friction.
The image that comes to mind is someone in the gym who wants to get stronger by progressive overload, but who adds so much weight that they can no longer lift at all.
With that in mind, today I want to offer something simple that you can start doing today to improve your reading.
Caveat: if you already have a system of note-taking, reviewing, summarizing, etc., and it’s working great for you, then you can skip this post.

This post is designed for readers who don’t currently make much use of pen or pencil while reading, or who have tried to do so but found it added too much friction and hindered their reading instead of helping it.
The Simple Practice Let’s take a brief look at the simple practice that will improve your reading, a brief defense of the practice, and some minor tips for making the most of it.
Here it is: after you read a chapter, jot down some notes, ideally in the book itself (if space allows).
